meta.title: Who really said "I Did It For My Own Pleasure. Then I Did It For My Friends. Now I Do It For Money"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Ad Reinhardt quoted the line in 1960 and named nobody. It is Ferenc Molnár’s, recorded by George Jean Nathan in 1932.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Did It For My Own Pleasure. Then I Did It For My Friends. Now I Do It For Money'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Reinhardt, not Molière, not Virginia Woolf. The playwright Ferenc Molnár said it around 1930; Nathan printed it in 1932.

answer.label: Not Ad Reinhardt — actually Ferenc Molnár
answer.sourceLine: The drama critic George Jean Nathan printed it in The Intimate Notebooks of George Jean Nathan (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1932), pp. 63–64, recalling a morning “two Summers ago” in a coffee-house garden in the Austrian Tyrol where Molnár, asked how he regarded his writing, answered “Like a whore.” Ad Reinhardt did use a version of the line — in a 1960 paper on artists’ ethics — but he set it in quotation marks and credited no one, and twenty-eight years separate his 1960 paper from Nathan’s 1932 printing.

source.excerpt: Like a whore. First, I did it for my own pleasure. Then I did it for the pleasure of my friends. And now—I do it for money.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the quip “was probably first constructed by Ferenc Molnár around 1930 and reported by George Jean Nathan in 1932”, and cites The Intimate Notebooks of George Jean Nathan (Knopf, 1932), pp. 63–64, noting it verified the page on paper.

Wikiquote ↗ reaches the same place by a different route: the “Writing is like sex” version sits in its Misattributed section for Woolf, and the note there transcribes the 1932 Nathan passage word for word.

Reinhardt’s own text is the reason his name stuck. QI quotes Rule 11 of his “Thirteen Rules of Ethical Conduct for Professional Fine Artists” — “It is not right for artists to think that painting is like prostitution, that ‘first you do it for love, then you do it for others, and finally you do it for money’” — from Art-as-Art: The Selected Writings of Ad Reinhardt ↗ (ed. Barbara Rose, University of California Press, 1991), p. 163. The inner quotation marks are his.

The Internet Archive’s catalogue confirms both books as QI describes them: the Nathan volume ↗ as New York: A. A. Knopf, 1932, and the Reinhardt collection ↗ as Berkeley: University of California Press, 1991.
source.excerptNote: That is the 1932 wording as Nathan set it down, quoted by Quote Investigator ↗ and reproduced independently on Wikiquote’s Virginia Woolf page ↗, which files the modern “writing is like sex” form under Misattributed and points back to the same book. Reinhardt’s 1960 version runs “first you do it for love, then you do it for others, and finally you do it for money” — already a quotation when he used it.

author.name: Ferenc Molnár
author.heading: About Ferenc Molnár
author.bio: Ferenc Molnár (born Ferenc Neumann in Budapest, 12 January 1878 – 1 April 1952) wrote Liliom, the play Rodgers and Hammerstein turned into Carousel, and the boys’ novel The Paul Street Boys, translated into dozens of languages. He was a working newspaperman before he was a dramatist, and the mordant, self-mocking register of this line — delivered with a monocle and a shrug — is exactly the pose his contemporaries recorded. He left Europe for the United States in 1940 and died in New York.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Four names get this line, and the evidence separates them cleanly: one said it first, two borrowed it openly, and two never said it at all.

items.why: Reinhardt used the saying in 1960 in Rule 11 of “The Artist in Search of a Code of Ethics” — but he wrapped it in quotation marks and named no source, which is how a man signals he is repeating something. QI ↗ notes that “in later years the words were sometimes attributed directly to him.”

The earliest Molière attribution QI ↗ can find is 1958, in a Nat Hentoff column quoting the novelist Ed Lacy. QI suggests Lacy may have misheard the less familiar name Molnár as Molière; no French or English source older than Molnár’s has been produced.

The “writing is like sex” wording circulates under Woolf’s name online. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed ↗, and QI calls the connection “rather recent” — possibly seeded by Woolf’s own, quite different, letters comparing publication to selling herself.

The Life photographer told a version in 1961 — “I drifted into photography like one drifts into prostitution” — and Leonard Nimoy recorded him telling it again as a story about someone else. Like Reinhardt, a user rather than an author.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Ferenc Molnár’s, about his own playwriting, recorded by George Jean Nathan in 1932; Reinhardt quoted it in 1960 and the quotation marks around it are his own — see Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Molnár was at the height of his European fame when he said it, and the joke works because he is the one telling it about himself: the man who wrote Liliom reducing his own career to a shrug and a monocle. Nathan, who collected exactly this kind of remark, printed it two years later.

What happened afterwards is the interesting part. The saying is portable — swap writing for painting, or photography, or sex — so each profession adopted it and each adopter picked up the credit. Reinhardt got it because he was quoting it in print in 1960; Woolf got it because the internet needed a woman writer to have said something bracing about money.
detailsBody: The chain QI assembles runs: Molnár to Nathan about 1930, printed 1932; Lynton Hudson’s Life and the Theatre in 1949, with “cocotte” for “whore”; Ed Lacy’s epigraph credited to Molière, quoted in the Village Voice in 1958; Reinhardt’s Rule 11 in 1960; Halsman in 1961; Weidman crediting Molnár again in 1962.

Reinhardt’s paper was read at the College Art Association meeting in New York on 28 January 1960 and, with further changes, at the Artists’ Club that April — a detail recorded in the editorial note to the essay in Art-as-Art. The rule it belongs to is a joke in its own right: the offending artist is to be “registered as a ‘lumpen artist’, issued an identity card, and dismissed with a suspended sentence.”
context.pull: Reinhardt put the words in quotation marks. Everyone who quoted him afterwards took the marks off.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the quip 'was probably first constructed by Ferenc Molnar around 1930 and reported by George Jean Nathan in 1932', and that attributions to Moliere and Virginia Woolf 'seem to be much weaker'.

QI quotes the 1932 Nathan passage verbatim ('Like a whore... First, I did it for my own pleasure...') and cites The Intimate Notebooks of George Jean Nathan, pages 63-64, Alfred A. Knopf, New York, verified on paper.

QI quotes Reinhardt's Rule 11 with the saying in internal quotation marks and no attribution, citing Art-as-Art: The Selected Writings of Ad Reinhardt, ed. Barbara Rose, University of California Press, 1991, page 163, and notes the paper was read in New York on 28 January 1960.
QI's earliest located Moliere attribution is a 1958 Village Voice column by Nat Hentoff quoting Ed Lacy, and QI suggests Lacy may have misheard 'Molnar' as 'Moliere'.

Wikiquote's Virginia Woolf page lists 'Writing is like sex. First you do it for love, then you do it for your friends, and then you do it for money' under Misattributed, and quotes the 1932 Nathan passage recording Molnar in full.
The Internet Archive catalogue record for The Intimate Notebooks of George Jean Nathan gives creator "Nathan, George Jean, 1882-1958", date 1932, publisher "New York : A.A. Knopf".
The Internet Archive catalogue record for Art-as-art: the selected writings of Ad Reinhardt gives creator "Reinhardt, Ad, 1913-1967", date 1991, publisher "Berkeley : University of California Press".

Wikipedia gives Ferenc Molnar's dates as January 12, 1878 - April 1, 1952, born Ferenc Neumann, a Hungarian-born author, stage director, dramatist and poet, who emigrated to the United States in 1940.
Wikipedia gives Ad Reinhardt's dates as December 24, 1913 - August 30, 1967, an American abstract painter and art theorist active in New York City.
